title: Before You Say “I Do,” Read This First: The Kind of Man Worth Waiting For Will Not Just Win Your Heart—He Will Help You Finish the Race to Christ
paragraphs:
Before You Say “I Do,” Read This First: The Kind of Man Worth Waiting For Will Not Just Win Your Heart—He Will Help You Finish the Race to Christ
The greatest love story is not about finding the perfect husband. It's about becoming so captivated by Jesus that you refuse to settle for anything that pulls your heart away from Him.
Every young Christian woman dreams about the future.
Maybe not always out loud.
Maybe not in front of everyone.
But somewhere between late-night prayers, wedding invitations, social media engagement posts, and quiet moments alone with God, the question whispers into the heart:
"Lord... who will I marry?"
It is one of the most emotional questions a woman can ask.
Not because she is desperate.
But because marriage is one of the greatest earthly covenants God ever designed.
The wrong person can slowly drain your faith.
The right person can encourage you to become more like Christ every single day.
That is why Scripture never begins with attraction.
It begins with worship.
Long before asking, "Is he handsome?"
God asks,
"Does he fear Me?"
Our culture tells young women to search for chemistry.
God tells them to search for character.
Culture celebrates butterflies.
Heaven celebrates holiness.
Those are not the same thing.
The Bible never teaches women to marry a perfect man.
It teaches them to marry a faithful one.

The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly describe the fear of God using the phrase יִרְאַת יְהוָה (Yir'at Adonai)—"the fear of the LORD." This is not terror but reverent awe, humble obedience, and joyful submission to God. Proverbs 9:10 says, "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." A man may possess education, success, charm, and ambition, yet if he lacks Yir'at Adonai, Scripture says he lacks the true beginning of wisdom itself.
One of the saddest mistakes many believers make is assuming that because someone attends church, they are spiritually mature.
Attendance is not transformation.
Knowledge is not surrender.
Even ministry involvement is not proof of intimacy with Christ.
Jesus Himself warned in Matthew 7:21, "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of My Father who is in heaven."
The issue has always been the heart.

The Apostle Paul commands believers in 2 Corinthians 6:14 not to be "unequally yoked with unbelievers." The image comes from agriculture: two oxen yoked together must pull in the same direction. Marriage joins two lives under one covenant. If one spouse walks toward Christ while the other walks toward self, the yoke becomes painful instead of fruitful.
Young Christian women often ask what they should look for in a husband.
The Bible gives surprisingly practical answers.
Look for a man whose private life matches his public faith.
Anyone can raise their hands during worship.
But who is he when nobody is watching?
Does he repent when he sins?
Does he confess quickly?
Does he fight temptation?
Does he seek accountability?
Does he hunger for Scripture?

Psalm 1 describes the blessed man whose "delight is in the law of the LORD." The Hebrew word for "delight" is חֵפֶץ (chephets), meaning deep pleasure, treasured desire, or cherished affection. God's Word is not merely something he reads; it becomes something he loves.
A godly husband is not merely informed by Scripture.
He is formed by it.
Look for a man who loves Jesus more than he loves you.
That sentence sounds strange until you understand the Gospel.
If you become the greatest love of his life, eventually you will disappoint him.
You were never designed to carry that weight.
Only Christ can.
When Jesus remains first, every other relationship finds its proper place.
Jesus said in Matthew 22:37, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind."
Everything else flows from that.
Look for humility.

The Greek word often translated "humility" is ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosynē)—a lowliness of mind that willingly places God above self and others above selfish ambition. Philippians 2 points to Christ Himself, who "humbled Himself" by becoming obedient to death on a cross.
Humility is not weakness.
It is strength surrendered.
A humble man apologizes.
He listens.
He receives correction.
He grows.
Pride destroys marriages long before adultery ever does.
Look for integrity.
Proverbs says, "The righteous who walks in his integrity—blessed are his children after him."
Integrity means he remains the same person whether people applaud him or ignore him.
He does not wear Christianity like a costume.
He lives it.
Look for kindness.
Not performative kindness.
Not romantic kindness.
Christlike kindness.
Ephesians 4:32 commands believers to "be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you."
How does he treat servers?
Children?
His parents?
People who disagree with him?
Enemies?
Character is revealed most clearly when there is nothing to gain.
Look for a servant.
Jesus completely redefined greatness.
In Mark 10:45 He declared,
"For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many."
If the King washed feet...
What excuse does any husband have for refusing to serve his wife?
Real biblical masculinity is never domination.
It is sacrificial leadership.
Christ loved the Church and gave Himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25).
That verse is often quoted at weddings.
Its weight is often missed.
Jesus did not merely provide.
He sacrificed.
Biblical headship is shaped like a cross.
Not a throne.
Look for emotional maturity.

The fruit of the Spirit listed in Galatians 5 includes love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. The Greek word for self-control is ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia)—the Spirit-enabled ability to govern one's desires instead of being ruled by them.
Can he control his anger?
His words?
His lust?
His spending?
His pride?
Marriage magnifies what already exists.
It rarely fixes what remains unrepented.
Look for repentance.
Everyone sins.
Everyone fails.
The question is never whether he falls.
The question is whether he runs back to Christ.
King David committed terrible sins, yet Acts 13:22 still calls him "a man after My own heart."
Why?
Not because David sinned less.
Because David repented deeply.
Psalm 51 remains one of the clearest portraits of genuine repentance ever written.
The Hebrew plea חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים (Channeni Elohim) means, "Be gracious to me, O God."
That cry still echoes through every redeemed heart today.
Do not chase potential.
Watch patterns.
Promises do not build marriages.
Habits do.
Love can be sincere while discernment remains necessary.
God never asks His daughters to ignore wisdom for romance.
Some women secretly believe marriage will complete them.
It will not.
Only Christ can.
Genesis says God created marriage before sin entered the world.
Marriage is good.
But it has always been a signpost pointing toward something greater.
Paul reveals in Ephesians 5 that marriage ultimately reflects Christ and His Church.
The earthly covenant exists because of the eternal covenant.
That changes everything.
Perhaps you are reading this after heartbreak.
Perhaps someone promised forever and disappeared.
Perhaps someone quoted Bible verses while breaking your trust.
Perhaps someone claimed to love God while treating you carelessly.
If that is your story, remember this:
People can misrepresent Jesus.
Jesus never misrepresents Himself.
He remains faithful.
The greatest Husband Scripture ever describes is Christ Himself.
He pursues the undeserving.
He protects the weak.
He forgives the guilty.
He sanctifies His Bride.
He never abandons those who belong to Him.
That is why every Christian marriage must begin there.
Not with rings.
Not with romance.
Not with dreams.
But with the cross.
Because only people transformed by grace can truly extend grace.
The world often asks, "How do I find the right person?"
The Gospel first asks,
"Are you becoming the kind of disciple who treasures Christ above everything else?"
That question changes how we date.
How we wait.
How we pray.
How we love.
Maybe today you are still waiting.
Do not mistake waiting for wasting.
God often prepares people in hidden seasons before entrusting them with visible blessings.
Isaiah 40:31 reminds us that those who wait upon the LORD renew their strength. Biblical waiting is never passive resignation; it is active trust.

If the Lord calls you into marriage, seek a man who is first seeking Christ. If He calls you to wait longer, trust that His wisdom exceeds your timeline. Your identity has never rested in a relationship status but in your union with Christ.
The greatest romance ever written did not begin with two people finding each other.
It began with a holy God pursuing sinners through the blood of His Son.
That is the story we all belong to.
That is why our theme will always remain true:
If this article challenged your heart, don't let it end here.
One faithful decision today can become a testimony that blesses generations tomorrow.
